turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the system's just thrown a wobbly again. Give me a second. Right, what's brought you in?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): So my heart's been doing this weird fluttery thing, and I get proper puffed out with it. We nearly didn't get here, the 49 was rammed and some bloke had a speaker on full blast.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I was on the wrong tab. Say that first bit again?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Palpitations. And I get breathless when they come. Mostly when I'm in bed at night.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Alex, his partner, we live together. It's been frightening at night, he sits bolt upright.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has it actually been going on?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): About three weeks. No, hang on, it was before reading week, so six weeks.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks? The screen just refreshed, I missed that. Six?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, six weeks. Not three.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Six weeks, and it's always worse the night before an exam or one of his Monday meetings.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not stress, though. I don't do stress. My supervisor's just obsessed with Harvard referencing, she docked me marks for a comma, which is ridiculous.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You do get wound up. Before every exam and those cafe meetings you're pacing the flat and snapping.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not stressed. I just like being ready, that's a completely different thing.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): The breathlessness, does it only come with the fluttering?

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the breathlessness comes with the palpitations. These six weeks, night-time's the worst, and it's bad before exams and before the Monday meetings. I do a few cafe shifts on top of the master's, so Mondays are stocktake.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain at all?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain, not even a twinge.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you blacked out, or felt you were about to?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I've never fainted. My mate Keiran went down at a gig in March, dramatic, but that's not me.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hasn't fainted. He just grips the duvet till it passes.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or a temperature?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough and no temperature. I feel alright in myself apart from this.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): How much caffeine are you getting through?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Coffee, about three cups a day. Actually it's five, if I'm being straight. And energy drinks, two a day, no, three, mostly Monster.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, Teams just pinged. How many energy drinks did you say?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Three a day. And five coffees. It's how I get through the reading, sadly.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, three's fair. The recycling's basically a Monster museum.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke or vape?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I vape. I've been doing it two years. Actually no, six years, I started at eighteen and I'm twenty-four.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any asthma, or problems with your heart before this?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Mild asthma. I use the brown inhaler, no, I don't, I never got on with the preventer. It's the blue one, salbutamol, two puffs when I need it.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He forgets it half the time. I'm not convinced he uses it when he actually needs it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies? Medicines, food, anything?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm allergic to.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): And medicines, apart from that inhaler? The list on screen looks empty, is that right?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the inhaler day to day. Last year the GP tried bisoprolol, one point two five milligrams, no, it was two point five. I stopped it after a week because I felt completely wiped out.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Family history? Heart disease, thyroid, that sort of thing? Sorry, this cursor's jumping.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Mum's got an underactive thyroid. She's also just bought a cockapoo and it ate the telly remote, which is a whole other saga.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell her about that blood test at uni.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh yeah. Last year the uni GP did thyroid bloods and said they were borderline. They didn't give me any tablets.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Borderline what, sorry? I lost the end of that.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): They never told me a number. Just borderline, and leave it alone.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen while this loads. Pulse is regular, ninety-two. Chest is clear, heart sounds normal, no murmur. Blood pressure's one eighteen over seventy-six and your oxygen is ninety-nine percent.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Is ninety-two bad? My watch shouts at me on the bus sometimes, but I think it just hates hills.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ninety-two resting is fine. I think this is probably palpitations stirred up by the caffeine and the vaping, maybe a few ectopics, but I don't want to miss a thyroid problem or an odd rhythm.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I'll book a twenty-four hour heart monitor, and I'll send you for thyroid bloods.

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): The thing is, each flutter only lasts about twenty seconds, and I've got an exam every single day next week. I can't be wired up for twenty-four hours, I'll rip the pads off in the first hour.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He really won't manage a monitor next week. The exams have him all over the place.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, that changes it. Scrap the twenty-four hour monitor for now. I'll do an ECG instead, and we'll still do the thyroid bloods.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the ECG and the thyroid test are alright and the palpitations haven't settled after your exams, we might arrange a twenty-four hour monitor then.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Meanwhile, try slow breathing when it starts, in for four and out for six, especially at night and before those meetings. And cut the energy drinks and the coffees right down, and ease off the vape if you can.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I did download a yoga app in January. Used it twice. The woman was so calm it annoyed me, which is ironic, ignore me.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in three weeks and we'll go through the results. If you get proper chest pain, or you collapse, don't wait on me, go to A&E.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Prior thyroid bloods were described as borderline, but transcript doesn't explicitly say borderline thyroid blood test result.
bad.text: Thyroid blood test reported as borderline (type=laboratory, status=completed)

omissions.text: Palpitations are mostly when he is in bed at night; partner says he sits bolt upright during episodes.
Each palpitation/flutter episode lasts about 20 seconds.
Negative finding: no presyncope/'felt you were about to' faint as well as no blackout/fainting.
Past history/investigation detail: last year uni GP said thyroid bloods were borderline and did not prescribe any tablets.
Bisoprolol was stopped because it made him feel 'completely wiped out'.
The initially planned 24-hour monitor was explicitly cancelled for now because he could not manage it during exam week.
